I understand that the right hon. leader of the Government and the right hon. leader of the Opposition have come to an agree-men whereby I am privileged to go on with
my Estimates this afternoon, and I wish to thank both right hon. gentlemen for their courtesy in arranging this matter.
I have been listening for some little time to the discussion of matters bearing on business and finance, which is something we are not accustomed to do in the Department of Militia and Defence. There we do not listen; we practise; our thoughts turn more to the practical end of things. The last time I had the opportunity of listening to a financial discussion I heard a speech from the lips of that distinguished soldier, General Joffre, the great leader of the French soldiers who have acquitted themselves so gloriously in the recent fighting. On that occasion General Joffre, a practical business man as well as a brilliant soldier, pointed out the desirability of union- between the French and British peoples, not only in the fighting, but in the financing of this great war, and he took the liberty of suggesting that it could be done by floating an Anglo-French loan in the United States, and he also suggested the possibility of Canada doing something along the same lines in order to- carry on the great struggle in which we are now engaged.
Before entering into details I should like to give a brief resume of the work of my department. I have not burdened the House much with elaborate explanations during the last three years when putting through the Militia Estimates, and I take this opportunity to thank the House for the confidence it has shown in the department. We are pleased to have all necessary inquiries made, and I am satisfied that the House will be pleased with the information it receives. The task in which we are now engaged is one that is second to none in the history of Canada from a business or financial point of view. Three great undertakings have been carried through in the Dominion. One was the Canadian Pacific railway, another t'be National Transcontinental railway, but these pale into insignificance compared with the magnitude of the financial operations connected with this great war. Canada was a peaceful nation trying to build up homes for her people, and to promote industries for their benefit. In connection with the expenditures on this war, the Government have had many more complicated problems to handle than had the Canadian Pacific railway or the National Transcontinental railway. These undertakings occupied years, and those engaged in them had ample time for elaborate preparations, with large staffs



them all. In 1914, we took steps to have fuses manufactured in Canada. Every firm that any one could even dream of as being likely to indulge in the manufacture of these commodities was approached, and not one firm in Canada could be induced by any offer of assistance to go into the manufacture of these fuses. Any one could see that fuses would be needed. Later on, an order came to the Shell Committee from the British Government for 4,000,000 fuses. I had nothing to do with this-as I have had nothing to do with the Shell Committee- other than to ask the same gentleman to make sure that the lowest possible prices were obtained. I may say that I knew that the raw material for these fuses-time fuses -cost, before the war, $1.90, which included 24 cents royalty to'the Krupp firm. This is the same fuse that we are making to-day. I realized that under the conditions prices would be almost sure to double, if not more, but still I thought that they should be obtained at that price. Imagine our surprise when Col. Bertram told me that they were asking $6 apiece for these fuses. I sent for Col. Allison and said to him that this price was absurd, that we should get them for easily half that, and so fire two shots instead of one at these gentlemen who are seeking to overthrow the liberties of the British Empire and of the French nation. Col. Allison brought the price down to $5.10; later, to $4.90, which is the lowest price for which I have heard of any company in the United States, the Morgans or any other, making fuses for the British Government. Later, Col. Allison brought the price down to $4.50, and, by still further organization, to $4.25. Contracts were made at this price of $4.25 for these time fuses. But, owing at least in part to the fact that a number of firms in the United States had been blown up, and there was more or less of the "German peril" idea abroad, they refused to take the contract, and it remained at $4.50. Thus there was a saving of 40 cents on each fuse, or a total saving to the British Government of $1,600,000 in that one deal alone.
Then the president of the Shell Committee informed us that a rush order had come in for No. 100 fuse for the high explosive shell. This is not a time fuse. All that we could ascertain about it was that it was being made in Great Britain for $3.75. A contract was let in the United States at $4

and I may say that Colonel Allison never heard of that contract until it had been let. Subsequently, a month later, a contract was let at $3.50, with the price of $4 to a firm
	,
in Canada, who, I believe, got their fuses largely made in the United States.
Speaking of these matters, I received thi3 morning from Colonel Skinner, head of the Colt's Patent Fire Arms Manufacturing Company of Hartford, Conn., the following:
28th February, 1916. To Major-General Sir Sam Hughes:
Dear General Hughes,

At the suggestion of Mr. Archie MacFarlane, the Canadian representative for the Colt's Company, I am sending you my affidavit covering details of sales Of machine guns and pistols to your Government at the beginning of the war and since. I have tried to cover the points named by Mr. MacFarlane, and trust that I have done so in a satisfactory manner.
Sincerely yours,
Wm. C. Skinner.
I,	William C. Skinner, of Hartford, Connecticut, chairman of the Board of Directors of the Colt's Patent Fire Arms Manufacturing Company, being duly sworn, do depose and say:
1.	That on account of personal friendship between Major General the Honourable Sir Sam Hughes- and myself, the Colt's Patent Fire Arms Manufacturing Company has given preference to Canada in regard to the execution of orders for machine guns and pistols, and particularly in the matter of giving the Government of Canada options for the purchase of machine guns, such options extending over a much greater length of time than the company has accorded to other governments.
2.	That on account of the promptitude of the Department of Militia of Canada in placing its first order for machine guns after the outbreak of war it was granted a price of $600, which was the price for similar guns and equipment to the United States government, and no sales of machine guns of similar type and equipment have been made to any other foreign government since the outbreak of war except at a higher price.
3.	That the price of the said machine guns and equipment as quoted to the Canadian Government was later advanced from $600 to $650, such increase being due to the greatly increased cost of labour and materials, and this advance in price applied to all other sales made by the company to other nations. A number of the sales made to other nations were for much larger quantities than were covered by orders from the Canadian Government.
4.	That the price charged the Canadian Government for automatic pistols, Cal. '45, namely $18.50, was the same price at which the company has sold to ^11 other governments since the outbreak of war with the exception of the Government of the United States, for which Government the pistol was expressly designed and with which Government the company has a special contract.
5.	That nothing was added to the selling price of machine guns, pistols or revolvers sold to the Canadian Government for commission or selling expenses and that the Canadian Government could not have obtained these these machine guns, pistols and revolvers from any other source at lower prices than those paid by it to the company.
William C. Skinner.

Sworn and acknowledged before me at the city of Hartford, Conn., this 28th day of February, 1916,
Arthur U. Ulrich,
'	Notary Public.
I wish to enter into the details of these matters as fully as possible. Another question which has arisen, and which has been discussed very much, is that concerning the Canadian trench shovel. This shovel was invented at the Swiss manoeuvres in 191213. It was realized in some quarters when this war broke out that it would Jbe a trench and shield war. I may recall that when war was declared I drew attention to the fact that the war was going to be a trench war, and that, at the Prime Minister's request, I sent a cablegram across the water dealing with this aspect of the matter. It was realized at the outbreak of the war that no troops could possibly advance against machine guns and rifles; and during the course of the fighting it has been proved over and over again that this cannot be done. It cannot be done and will not be done, unless at the conclusion of the war auxiliary means of covering the advance are provided. The shovel to which I have refered has since formed the model for the trench and shield shovels, some for one, . some for two, and some for three men, used by the French, Prussians and British in trench work. Inquiry was made from the United States and British firms as to the prices at which these shovels could be manufactured, but the prices were all too high. The lowest price I got at first was between $4 and $5; the highest price was $6. After a number of experiments had been carried out, the Midvale Company evolved a process of making them more cheaply, and they came down in their price to $1.35. The Midvale Company, in order to cover themselves legally in the premises, asked the inventor and the minister if there was any royalty; and the reply in each case distinctly was that there was no royalty whatever. The Russian Government offered the inventor 5 cents a shovel on 1,000,000 shovels, but the offer was declined. The question of delivery arose. The shovels had to be shipped to Col. Allison, or to some one named by him,, by whom the^ were transferred to this side of the line at no cost to the Canadian Government. When the first contingent sailed the straps and fastenings were not ready, and these shovels were left in England. They were not the only things that were left in England at that time. Fifty-one motor trucks were left
there, as well as wagons, harness, saddles, water-carts, boots, field kitchens and valise equipment. When the second division went across, I put my foot down. Our goods had stood the wear and tear of training in England, and I could not see why they should not stand similar conditions in France. We took steps, therefore, to secure as far as possible- the use of our own materials at the front.
The board which was subsequently requested to look into this matter reported that the Canadian supplies were thoroughly serviceable.
Another matter which has been exercising public attention to a considerable degree is that of the Ross rifle. I shall not go into the history of this matter, for it has been gone over again and again in days gone by. Suffice it to say that the Lee-Enfield was not a success in South Africa. The Ross rifle, having a straight, pull, had commended itself to many; trade-rivalry sprung up; opposition came from people who opposed the spending of any-money on rifles, and, for this and other-reasons, the Canadian rifle was bitterly opposed. The Mark 3 Ross rifle is an excellent weapon; it has the same calibre as the British rifle, and takes the same ammunition. The fact that the chamber-not the groove or the barrel-of the Ross rifle was two-thousandths of an inch smaller than the chamber of the Lee-Enfield was claimed by some to be the cause of the jamming of the cartridge in the barrel. The reason was this: The Canadian-proved rifle is the same as the British-proved rifle. The steel elastic limit of the British rifle is only 48,000 lbs. to the square inch, while that of the Ross is 76,000 lbs. With the Lee-Enfield a proof charge of 50,000 pounds caused the chamber of the rifle to be raised .462 instead of .460. However, the Canadian rifle has been reamed out and enlarged to .464, and, as the British rifle has been similarly treated, the two rifles are now the same size. The difference of two-thousandths of an inch made it more practicable for both rifles to take the defective cartridges which were found all through the. service. These rifles were reamed out because different brands of ammunition issued by the British Government were found to be defective. As they contained: brass, and were very soft, they would stick in the gun when they were fired. Frequent tests have been made with this ammunition, and in every instance the Canadian rifle has gone more rounds than the;

Lee-Enfield before jamming. I may mention that that bad ammunition was all withdrawn from the lines, and no trouble has since been experienced. No charge of jamming in either rifle has been made for many a day.
Where is Canadian ammunition made?
At the city of Quebec; also at points this side of Montreal.
Is there any truth in the rumour that it is the intention to transfer the ammunition factory from Quebec to Lindsay?

The factory at
.Quebec will remain there.
Do I understand the hon. minister to say that the Ross rifle has given absolute satisfaction?

I will make that
clear before I get through; if I do not do so, I shall be glad if my hon. friend will repeat the question. I shall not go into the details of the arguments advanced by those who have opposed the Ross, rifle, but I wish to call attention to a strange incident that occurred at the time of the battle of St. Julien. It having been found that a number of the rifles were jamming, ten questions were circulated among the Canadians, as follows:
1.	Do you find the Lee-Enfleld better on account of its being lighter?
2.	Do you find the Lee-Enfield to be handier on account of its shortness?
3.	Do you find that the bolt in the Lee-Enfield does not jam as .much as in the Ross?
4.	Is the aim not quicker with the Lee-Enfield owing to the sights?
5.	Do not the heavy lugs guarding the foresight on the Lee-Enfield give an approximate aim at night which the ring on the Ross does not?
6.	Does not the magazine of the Lee-Enfleld hold ten cartridges while the Ross holds only five?
So far as that last question is concerned, I may say that every rifle in the world, the Lee-Enfleld included, has five cartridges in the magazine. The next questions are:
7.	Is it not true that the magazine of the Lee-Enfield allows for cleaning, while that of the Ross does not?
8.	Does not the charger clip guide on the Ross allow too much play, making loading difficult?
I may say that not one of the suggestions made in these questions is justified. The next question is:
' 9. Does not the bayonet on the Ross work loose in rapid firing?
fSir Sam Hughes.]	.
The same may be true of any rifle. The last question is:	.
10. Is not the bayonet too short and thick?
This question I shall take up later. These ten questions were circulated in the Canadian division just before the battle of Ypres. If they were not circulated by some person in the hope of causing the Ross rifle to be distrusted, I should like to know what they were circulated for. The fact stands out that the Canadian forces, armed with Canadian rifles, held at St. Julien as no troops ever held before in the history of the world. There was some bad ammunition, and undoubtedly some of the rifles did jam, just as the British rifles jammed. Owing to the jamming of their Lee-Enfields, two British regiments were forced to retire after firing scarcely a shot. They had this bad ammunition, and their rifles jammed. The Durhams and Yorks, two of the finest regiments in the British service, were fighting with rifles that were useless, owing to the condition of the ammunition, and were forced to retire at various points, just as the other regiments were forced to retire at various points, not because of the men, but because of the bad ammunition that was served out to them.
,,At Festubert the Canadian Division, armed with the Ross rifle and fair ammunition, met with grand success, advancing 21 miles, and it was the only advance made along the whole line. The troops armed with the Lee-Enfleld made no advance, and that is charged up to bad ammunition. At Givenchy, our troops weTe armed with the Lee-Enfield, and, as is well known, we did not succeed in making an advance there on account of the bad ammunition. With regard to the bayonet it is now giving general satisfaction. I have this report here from Colonel Helmer on the bayonet: Memorandum re Bayonets, Ross Rifle.
1.	The Ross rifle bayonet was adopted with the idea of furnishing a combined tool and weapon ; being of the knife pattern and strongly constructed, it fulfils both requirements.
2.	No criticisms have been received from overseas regarding this bayonet, except that it is too short; but it must not be forgotten that the fighting length of the Ross rifle and bayonet
1 combined is equal to the Lee-Enfield and American rifles, i.e., long rifle, short bayonet, short rifle, long bayonet.
3.	Extremely long bayonets such as the French, Russian, and German, are inconvenient to carry, and for penetrating purposes none of them is superior to the Ross rifle except the French, which is of the stiletto type but useless for other purposes.
4.	Long bayonets, as compared with short, are.a decided disadvantage in a fight, in that they are less easily carried. In addition if a man " gets home " with a long bayonet, the wea-

pon is likely to go clean through the body and protrude, making extraction difficult and placing the man, who has momentarily succeeded, at the mercy of any one who attacks him. " A short quick jab and get clear " is the safest rule in bayonet fighting, and this is difficult with a long bayonet and rifle.
5.	The honourable the minister has given instructions that the bayonets for overseas are to be ground so as to provide a fine sharp point. It is understood that these instructions are now being carried out at the factory and inspection branch. This will eliminate any reasonable ground for criticism.
R. A. Helmer, Colonel,
Director of Musketry.
The bayonet was designed a number of years ago under the direction of my predecessor. We call it the Lake bayonet, because it was designed by General Lake, one of the best soldiers in the British Empire, and who is now in Mesopotamia. The Committee on Small Arms assisted General Lake in designing this bayonet. The one objection I had' to this bayonet was that it had a bulge at the point, but we have now had the bulge removed, and all the soldiers of the Canadian Division think that it is as perfect a weapon as there is in the world. To show what it can do, I need only mention that at St. Julien 2,000 Canadians entered a wood one night against 7,000 Germans, and only 1,000 Germans left the wood alive.
What is the present status of the Ross Rifle? Is it popular with the soldiers at the front?

All reports that 1
have received are to the effect that it is giving splendid satisfaction. Only a short time ago, a gentleman came to me with a letter from his son at the front, saying what a splendid weapon it was. The Ross rifle, in fact, is such a splendid success that the Canadian soldier has to sleep on it or the British soldier would steal it from him. Now that the bad cartridges have been eliminated, there is no trouble with either of the rifles being used at the front.
Then the statement in the Canadian Courier last year that the Ross rifles were discarded by our boys is untrue?

The- rifles were not discarded. As the House will understand, a number of our rifles were lost at St. Julien, and the first division were then given the British rifle. I do not know whether the first division have yet received the new weapon we are making, but as soon as the rifles are made the whole Canadian
army will be armed with the Ross rifles. At the . present time all our troops except the first division are using the Ross.
In regard to medical examiners, I might point out that we have now a new system. .Under the old system we found that recruiting was greatly embarrassed by reason of the fact that there was only one examiner in each district. We Lave altered that, and now the officer in command can appoint an examiner in any centre to examine recruits. The examiner is given fifty cents for each recruit examined. This new system is more economical, and much more convenient to the boys.
When did this new arrangement go into effect?
About a month ago.
Examiners only get fifty cents a man?
That is all they ask.
If all the minister's expenses were as economical as that we should have little to complain about.

I think we are enlisting the sympathy of the medical men. They have done splendid work, not only the military examiners, but civilian doctors too. I understand from my deputy that fifty cents per man is all they wish to take. They want to deal fairly and squarely with the country.

What was the previous system of medical inspection?
- Sir SAM HUGHES: The medical officer attached to each regiment would go all over his district examining recruits. It took the examiner fin my county about five weeks to cover his district.
How was he paid under the old system?
He got his regular pay, and travelling expenses.
Has the regulation in regard to height been altered?
We still have the old regulation. I may say that we are raising a couple of bantam regiments.

It was said that at Kingston last year there were a number of soldiers in the camp who had been passed by doetors not connected with the militia. After they had been in the camp for a considerable length of time, these men were

re-examined by the military .doctor, and some of them rejected. I understand that these outside doctors got $2 a piece for every recruit they accepted. Is there any truth in this report?

I think there is
more or less truth in the statement of my hon. friend. That is partly why we have adopted this new system. It will prevent anything of that kind happening again, and will expedite the work generally.
With regard to recruiting officers. Last year, when I was out of the country-I am not shirking any responsibility in this matter, but am just mentioning that it was done when I was in England-recruiting officers were appointed all over the country, whether military men or not. In many instances these men were excellent officers, but in other cases they were absolutely useless, and yet were kept on pay. In the month of November last we adopted a new system of recruiting. We issued the order that all these officers must attach themselves to an overseas battalion or retire, and most of them have since undertaken overseas service. We have an officer supervising the whole work, with headquarters here at Ottawa.	.
With regard to the billeting of troops, I am sure that our new system of billeting the boys in the small centres has met with general approval. The tendency hitherto has been to keep these troops in the larger centres, and that of course did nothing towards creating any local, spirit. Under our new system there is hardly a county in Canada to-day that has not soldiers billeted all over the district. I am pleased to learn from both sides of the House, and from men of all shades of politics, that our new system of billeting is giving satisfaction. Unfortunately, one or two officers on their own responsibility undertook to order the men into larger centres. This was done without the knowledge of headquarters, and as soon as we found out we promptly stopped it.
Schools of instruction had been opened in every division, and also in cities such as Ottawa, for example. Recently, a number of members on both sides of this House, animated with the laudable desire to acquire a knowledge of drill so that they would be prepared in case of necessity, desired to have a school of instruction open-' ed for their benefit at Ottawa. Some of these gentlemen were men up in years, business men not accustomed to getting up
fMr. Turriff.]
early in the morning, such as my venerable friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner); my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) and my hon. friend from Missisquoi (Mr. Kay), were also in the class. I believe they all managed to impress the instructor so favourably that he is giving them all a certificate of some kind or another; I do not know just what the details are. I am sure that there is not a man of them who, altogether apart from the war, does not regret that he did not start training when he was a boy, just for the benefit to be got out of it. It makes them better men.	.
There is another matter to which I desire to draw attention, and that is the question of promotion. There are three forces, the forces in Canada, the forces in England, and the forces at the front. It goes without saying that the heart of every good fellow in the country is with the boys in the firing line. The soldiers in England have no claim to more favourable consideration than the soldiers in Canada; if any favours arq to be given, they should go to the boys in the firing line. We had not a definite system until recently. No one ever dreamed that the war was going to last so long, otherwise we would have adjusted matters earlier. But we- have now got the matter on a proper footing, and the boys at the front will no longer have reason to complain in regard to lads who were their juniors in service when they left Canada getting priority in any company or regiment. In other words, the first consideration in the matter of promotion will be for the boys in the firing line. We will regard the forces in England and the forces in Canada as on the same footing I can see no reason why a man training at Shorncliffe should be given consideration in preference to the boys in the camps in Canada. I believe that that is a course which will meet with universal approval. As the House knows, promotions are made on the recommendation of the commanding officer of each regiment.
I might add that the same holds good in regard to honours for heroic conduct in action; we do not interfere in any sense whatever, though, of course we rejoice when we hear of a marrwinning meritorious recognition.
All the little difficulties in connection with the Valcartier camp ground are being satisfactorily settled. I will now present to the House a return of 29th February, 1916, showing the number of troops enrolled in the Dominion of Canada. In No.
1 district, which includes western Ontario,
MATJOTT 9 I91fi
there are 23,560; in No. 2 district (Toronto), 60,360; in No. 3 district (eastern Ontario), 27,856; making a total for the province of Ontario of 110,676, and nearly all are in readiness for the front.
In No. 4 district (Montreal), there are 22,926 soldiers; in No. 5 district (Quebec), 5,212, a total for the province of Quebec of 28,138.
In No. 6 district, which includes the Maritime Provinces, there are 24,198 soldiers enrolled-I have not the total for each province separately. In No. 10 district (Manitoba and Saskatchewan), there are 50,710; in No. 11 district (British Columbia), 24,368; in No. 13 district (Alberta), 24,424; the total for the four western provinces being 100,002.
Exclusive of officers, therefore, the total number of soldiers enrolled and on duty is 263,114. The number of officers is 10,468, which brings the total to about 275,000 troops, ready for overseas service.
Reference has been made to patronage. Every one knows that so far as the Department of Militia is concerned, the patronage list practically vanished at the outbreak of the war. If any grocer in the riding of any hon. member happens to get an extra bit of patronage, I do not know anything about it; we have not time to bother with such small things.

It is all very well
for the minister to say that there is no patronage list, but it is the case that when supplies are needed for the troops it is the friends of the Government who get the contracts. If the hon. minister is not responsible, who is?

In my own town, which is in the district under the officer commanding at Kingston-the district of my hon. friend is under the officer commanding at Halifax-two or three honest Grits are-I will not say enriching themselves-but getting a fair share of contracts.
Will the minister tell us how many Grits are getting a share in the town from which I come?
Are there any there?

I had a majority of 79 at the last election, and I will double it at the next election. Not a single Liberal has got a dollar's worth from the Militia Department, and at present we have 500 soldiers there.
I am glad there are so many soldiers, but I say, and I challenge contradiction, that we have not interfered. We have no time to look after the peddling of groceries.

There' is no use in my hon. friend saying that there is no patronage list. If the men who have charge of the distribution of these matters have a patronage list, then my hon. friend is not stating a fact. The minister can settle the question by giving directions to carry out what he says is his view.

My hon. friend
knows that so far as headquarters is concerned, and I challenge contradiction, we have not a patronage list in connection with our contracts. I do not know anything about these local affairs; it is the first time that my attention has been called to them. I have had complaints over and over again from Conservative members of Parliament who demanded my scalp because I had let Grits get contracts in various centres. The Prime Minister has been bombarded, and I have been bombarded with letters from Tory friends, because contracts have gone to Grits; I have had ten complaints of that character for the one I have had from Grits. But I have not paid any attention to them. They cannot all get contracts, and complaints about groceries are not woTth attention.

Last year I happened to be a member of a committee that investigated certain matters connected with the Militia Department and an officer came before that committee and distinctly swore 'that there was a patronage list in the department. That statement was made under oath.

We had a patronage list in the department before the war broke out, but so far as I know, after the war broke out, that patronage list received no consideration. The cases of a number of gentlemen, who had obtained contracts were reported to me, and I found that two of the firms, about which there was the most talk, were Grit firms, and representations were made that they should not get contracts. I refused to entertain any such objections.

The statement made before that committee by an officer of the department was that at that time, last spring, when the war was on, there was,

and had been for months, a patronage list in the department. The question is, is there, or is there not, a patronage list in the department? My hon. friend says there is not, which indicates, I assume, that the minister thinks that the proper way to do business is to dispense with such a list. Has there been a change since last year; has the patronage list been abolished since last March?

I know nothing about a patronage list last year. I know that there was a patronage list before the campaign came on, and I am not sure that I was very much enamoured of it. There has been no patronage list in connection with this war in the Militia Department-as far as I am concerned,, or as far as any officer with whom I am in touch is concerned.

The minister evidently could not have heard what took place in the Public Accounts Committee yesterday morning, when Mr. Brown, the purchasing agent of the department, stated there .was a patronage list, and that it had been made up after 1911. We asked him if he could produce it, and he said he could. We expect to have it before the committee tomorrow morning. He told us that down to last May he had bought from that patronage list and that since May he has been buying under the instructions, of the War Purchasing Commission. They send instructions to him, and when they want him to buy a certain article they tell him how to do it. Sometimes he buys from his own patronage list and sometimes he buys from a list of names that the War Purchasing Commission has given to him.
That is all under the War Purchasing Commission; I have nothing to do with that.
But it is done by the minister's department, and, his own purchasing officer swore to it yesterday.
Only recently the hon. member, for Ottawa berated me very severely because certain Liberals were getting contracts from my department.
You could not satisfy the member for Ottawa.

Let me say here that ever since this war began I have refused to allow patronage or politics to influence me in any shape, manner, or form, in regard to the appointment of men to office,
[Mr. Macdonald.!
or the awarding of contracts. Unfortunately, some of my Conservative friends say -that I have appointed too many Liberals. As long as they are good men it makes nodifference what their politics may be, but once they show that they are not out they go, whether they are Liberals or Conservatives. As far as the peddling arohnd of #200 or #300 worth of lumber or potatoes is concerned^ I have not given any attention to that, and I do not intend to. If I cannot trust my officers to look after things-of that kind they are not fit for their jobs.
Mr. W. M. 1IARTIN: Does the hon gentleman know anything about a patronage list in the city of Regina?
I do not know anything about it. How could you expect me to keep such things as that in my head?

I know that in the city I reside in no person but a Conservative can serve a meal to a soldier, and I am told that no person but a Conservative can shave-a soldier. The minister knows the trouble that developed in Regina some months ago in respect to the patronage system that existed there.	[DOT]
Who found it out?

I do not know whether the-minister found it out or not, but there is a great deal more, I believe, that might be-told and that the minister does not know.
If the minister does not want to go into it now we might take it up at some other time.

I would like to get through before six o'clock. I may say that we have carried out our ideas with regard to the development of our citizen soldiers. There is a tendency in many lands to place-the citizen soldier in a subordinate position to that of the regular soldier. My idea always has been that the citizen soldier, properly trained, is superior to the man who-is not properly trained, and this country has exemplified that fact. We have followed certain original ideals and ideas, and we have tried to hold a firm hand. Our decisions have to be rendered rapidly, because there are questions coming up every day, and we have always tried to be fair. I think I am justified in saying that every one of our decisions, and actions, has met with the approval of the men against whom they necessarily had to be directed at the time. There are only one or two instances in which our decisions have met with opposition. We have necessarily had to offend some contractors who wanted favours at-the hands of the department and some offi-

cers who were seeking places which the officers of my department thought they were not entitled to. There are certain other people who have raised disturbances but they are comparatively few in number, and, taking it all in all, I cannot but express my appreciation of the splendid assistance which the people of this country have given us in the strenuous work which the war has. imposed upon us.
I ;want to express my appreciation of the treatment accorded me on this side of the House by my Conservative friends. If any of my Conservative friends asked me to do anything which it was not possible to do, or to have done in their ridings which could not be done, when I explained the case to them, in every instance, I found them absolutely square and sympathetic and quick to see my difficulties. I want also to express my appreciation of the attitude of my hon. friends on the Liberal side of the House, who have been, all in all, very fair in this matter. Some of them have been more than fair and there have been, very few who have not been straight and just in their attitude towards me. I wish to express my appreciation to these gentlemen for their conduct in the premises.
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.

Militia and Defence-allowances active service, $100,000.

Mr. Chairman, before you go into the consideration of this item, I would like to make a few general observations with reference to the very mild and gentle speech delivered this afternoon by the Minister of Militia and Defence.^ I am a great admirer of the minister, because he has the most wonderful faculty of coming before the House of Commons, shooting off a lot of hot air, getting it into the newspapers the next morning, and getting away with it.
His organization is perfect.

Yes, and I think he has surpassed himself this afternoon; he has out-Hughed Hughes and Allison put together. If I could sum up his arguments under headings, I would say that the first heading is that there have been no politics and no patronage in the conduct of the affairs of the Department of Militia and Defence since the beginning of the war in August, 1914. In fact, I do not think he discussed anything regarding his department prior to that date, and therefore I do not intend to refer to anything prior to that date myself. I want to call my hon. friend's attention to a few matters which took place about a year ago, and I am sure my hon. friend's memory can go back as far as that, because he has told us of things which have happened as far back as the outbreak of the war. He has told us that there have been no patronage and no patronage lists, and that he has bought things from Grits and Tories, from everyone who had anything to sell. Now, I wondeT what he has to say about a few of the war purchases that we investigated in the Public Accounts Committee last session.
Let us take, for instance, the purchase ol binoculars. There is in the city of Ottawa a very estimable gentleman, Mr. Birkett, whose father is a hardware merchant, and I believe a very honourable one, a man who at one tifhe-occupied a seat in this House. This young man, according to the evidence, was a clerk in his father's business, and he never saw a binocular in his life except to look through it. He would not know anything about a 6 millimetre binocular or a 10 or 12 millimetre one any more than I would. Nevertheless this young man formed himself into a company called the Ottawa Supply Company, which was put on the patronage list. This company could not purchase binoculars themselves, because they did not know how to go about it, so they went to our good friend Sam Bilsky, who is a Liberal, and who knows how to buy binoculars; they allowed him a commission of $5 apiece, and they went down to New York and bought a lot of cheap binoculars at prices ranging from $7.50 to $25 each. They brought these binoculars to Canada and handed them over to one of the boys, and the Government bought the binoculars at $10 more than the original price. There was thus a rake-off of several thousand dollars. I do not care whether you call it patronage or not, but if Birkett had not got his name on the patronage list, he would not have been able to sell binoculars to the Government.

The Government would not
buy from Bilsky.

Certainly not. Bilsky
was a Grit, and although Bilsky tried over and over again, as only gentlemen of his race know how to try, he could not get his name on the patronage list.

If my memory serves me aright-and I think it will be found fairly accurate-it was Colonel Hurdman,

a gentleman whom I retained in my service, who made this deal, whether good, bad or indifferent, and the matter was taken up later on by Mr. Mason. The whole thing was started by Colonel Hurdman, a Lib-'eral in whom I had confidence.

The hon. minister need not hit back at us this evening after being so kind to us this afternoon. Colonel Hurdman is not on trial. The people of this country do not care two straws who Colonel Hurdman' is or whether he ever was in the business at all.

Colonel Hurdman
had no list whatever; he made this deal off his own bat.
I can give that a flat denial.
The hon. gentleman certainly can, if he wishes.
So far as the county of Peterborough is concerned it is absolutely untrue.

The hon. gentleman will have a chance to air his views in a little while. This is a free-and-easy argument;
we are in committee, and the night is young, and all may have an opportunity of expressing their views. What I say is that from one end of Canada to the other it is nothing but politics and the patronage list. Why, down in New Brunswick the patronage committee even appoint commissioned officers up to lieutenants. If a man wants an appointment as lieutenant in the province of New Brunswick he goes to the patronage committee.
Did that occur in the case of Major Anderson?
He is a major.
Can the hon. gentleman give one solitary name in New Brunswick to establish what he says?
Yes.

I would like to
hear it.
In Victoria and Madawaska-

The commanding
officer at Sydney is a Liberal, and so is the commanding officer at Moncton; Colonel Borden at Halifax is a Liberal, and so is the next officer under him. Colonel Mc-Avity of St. John is a Liberal, and so is every man of them in the Maritime Provinces, except Colonel McLeod.

That is more hot air.
Any man who lives in New Brunswick knows that the minister has been misinformed-to put it that way-because those who want appointments must go to the patronage committee. There are Liberals in the province of New Brunswick who have commissions, but they had to go to the patronage committee. Every time the minister has referred to this matter he has spoken of Colonel McAvity and Major Anderson. They are good men-such good men that they could not get around them. But whether it is a commission to be given or an order to be placed for meat or lumber, it is all politics there from beginning to end.
The minister spent a good deal of his time in defending his own department with regard to certain matters, and I am not going into them all. He went a long way out of his way, I thought, to defend Colonel Allison. When he was making that defence there came to my mind the well-known words of Shakespeare:	" The lady doth
protest too much, methinks." One can hardly understand why it should be necessary for the minister to take half or three-

quarters of an hour of the time of Parliament in defence of Colonel Allison. If Colonel Allison is all right, why not say so and let it go at that? Let me point out to the minister one of the cruel things in this world-at least from his standpoint: he must think it a cruel thing that such an angel in disguise as Colonel John Wesley Allison should be so maligned by ordinary people. Well, my experience of life has been rather the other way. I have very seldom found the real, true, honest man of this world maligned by anybody. And when I find reports with regard to a person coming from every point of the compass, all tallying exactly and all along the same line, I naturally come to the conclusion that there is a little truth in them. Where there is so much smoke there is sure to be fire. But the minister says that Colonel Allison is an honest man-I think he said he was the only honest man he had met since the war began. At least he said he was the most honest of all the men he had met, if there can be degrees of honesty, and I presume' there can be. But, besides being the most honest man, Colonel Allison, it seems, is also the most able. Why it is evident that the minister could never have carried on this war successfully-and I want to give him all the credit that is coming to him; he has shown a lot of energy and has done some great hustling; we on this side give him credit for all that-had it not been for the great assistance he has received from Colonel Allison. Judging from what we have heard this afternoon, had it not been for this gentleman, the minister would not have succeeded in getting anywhere; there would have been no Canadian overseas force but for him. The minister tells us that Colonel Allison has saved $50,000,000 since the war began, and would not take a cent. What is the use of the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) racking his brains and getting grey-headed over the question of raising money for this war, when all that is necessary is to bring on this wizard, Colonel Alliston, and let him wave his magic wand, and bring forth $50,000,000 when it is needed. Why, the minister has not treated this colleague of his right. Instead of having Colonel .Allison down there in the United States he ought to have him here, running the whole show. I am afraid, maybe, some of his colleagues would object to Colonel Allison running the show, and some of his followers also. Looking at the faces of some of the fol-' 
lowers of the Government, when the minister was extolling the virtues of his friend, I thought I noticed on some of them indications of dissent. That may have been an optical delusion, but some feeling was patent in their faces as the minister was telling of the virtues of Colonel Allison. Well, we have invited Colonel Allison to come before the Public Accounts Committee, and we will have an opportunity to judge for ourselves whether the minister's opinion of this gentleman is right or wrong, coloured or not-that is, from our standpoint, and I admit that we are very much below the plane of the ministe>-The minister endeavoured this afternoon to free Colonel Allison from any suspicion of wrong-doing. Well, the minister had better wait until a charge is made before he attempts to put up a defence. But let me call attention to something that was brought out in the Public Accounts Committee yesterday morning. A man named Nash, a tailor, I think, of Morrisburg, said that in the early days of the war he was requested by Mr. Chambers who, I have learned, is a very active gentleman in the Conservative organization of the constituency that I have mentioned, to give Colonel Morgan some assistance in the tailoring line. He consented, and, with that end in view, went to Colonel Allison's office, where he met Colonel Morgan and two or three merchants, from Redfield, New Jersey. These gentlemen, one of whom was a Mr. Eismer, had twenty or twenty-five samples of all kinds of army clothing-caps, greatcoats, tunics, trousers, knickerbockers, handkerchiefs, shirts, shoes, blankets. Upon these samples was stamped the firm name and the price. Evidently the gentlemen who came here from New Jersey were not trying to deceive anybody, for there were the. samples, with the name of the firm and the price of the goods stamped upon them. But the Conservatives of Morrisburg employed this tailor to go to Colonel Allison's office and change these labels. He cut the labels off, and put on other labels from which he had removed his own name, simply leaving the label blank-" white linen," he called them. The number and the price, I think, appeared on the label. Mr. Nash does not know exactly what was done, but he heard them talking about the price that was going on one of these labels. The price that was on the manufacturer's label was $3.50-this was a pair of trousers-and he says that they were talking about putting on a price something over $4. When we asked him why they were removing these labels, he

said they told him that they did not want the Germans to know from whom the goods had been bought. A little later in the investigation he said that these were samples, and that he heard them direct the stenographer to address them to Sir Sam Hughes at Ottawa. I asked him if he was afraid that the Germans might capture some of the British soldiers who were wearing these trousers, and subsequently trace their purchase back to United States manufacturers. He said he hardly thought so, because these goods were only samples. Then I asked him if he thought the price would scare the Germans, but he had entirely receded from the German theory.
' These samples were going to the Minister of Militia; it was supposed that from them the Government of Canada would purchase goods. The manufacturer was perfectly willing to leave the price upon the goods, so that everybody should see it. In Col. Allison's office, by Col. Morgan, his associate and friend, these tags were cut off and other tags put on upon which other prices were placed. We have not got any further than that; I do not know whether they succeeded in getting orders.
The hon. gentleman is in error when he says that other prices were placed upon the labels.
The witness swore that he heard them talking about putting another price upon this particular pair of trousers-more than $4.
The hon. gentleman just now said that other prices were placed on these tags.
Certainly.
That is not so.

I will admit that the Ghairman of the Public Accounts Commit-dee, by his ingenuity, did everything he could to keep that evidence from coming out. But he got it, and now the public is getting it. The Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee is now seeking to draw a herring across the trail.
The hon. gentleman is stating what is not true.

That will not help
matters one particle. I tell my hon. friend Tight here that we know our rights in the Public Accounts Committee just as well as he does, and we know our rights in this committee just as well as he does. He will
not help the Estimates through by any such conduct as this.	'
My hon. friend said a moment ago-and Hansard will bear me out in this-that different prices were placed upon these tags.
Yes; and they were.

The evidence was
that there was a price of $3.50 on one pair of trousers, and that no other prices were put on. As my hon. friend says, the witness heard different prices mentioned.

Is that not a nice distinction? Is the Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee not covering himself with glory by making a statement of that kind? The Solicitor General will have to resign if my hon. friend takes his place in the hair-splitting business. With all 'the ingenuity that the Solicitor General possesses, he never could make an argument like that; he never could draw so fine a distinction as that. What do you suppose they cut these tags off for? What was the object of taking these articles into Colonel Allison's office and changing the tags? They say it was done to fool the Germans; do you think anybody in Canada is fool enough to be fooled by a reason like that? Hardly. The minister knows better; everyone of his followers around him knows better; even the Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee knows better. He knows that men do not .do things like that without a purpose, and he knows that the purpose of these men was to deceive somebody-and that somebody was the Government of Canada. Whether they succeeded or not, I do not know. We will try to find out.
The hon. minister told also about the wonderful honesty of Col. Allison in purchasing Colt revolvers and pistols. I shall not go into that to-night, for I know that there will be another opportunity of going into it more thoroughly. The hon. gentleman tries to justify the throwing away of thousands of dollars of the people's money because of something that was done in 1899 or 1900. It is the tu quoque argument over again; if somebody else steals, we have the right to steal. That is the answer that has been given to every statement which we have made on this side of the House since 1911.

May I correct my hon. friend? I did not say that if somebody else had the right to steal, we also have the right to steal, but that if some others had

the right to put on a commission, we might have justification for putting on a commission, but we did not do it.

Then I will modify my assertion by using the word "commission" instead of the word "steal." The hon. gentleman says: "We did not do it." Has my hon. friend forgotten the evidence given by two reputable witnesses before Sir Charles Davidson's commission in Ottawa, one of them a representative of Mr. Birkett and the other a representative of the Ketchum Company? Two hardware firms in this city swore at the very time the minister was buying these revolvers at $18.50 that they were able to buy them at a discount of 10, 5 and 2i per cent, which brought the price down to $15.05; it was either $15.05 or $14.05. One of these firms bought one pistol, - and the other two. And Colonel Allison, who was buying them by the thousand, paid $3.50 more for his pistols than did these two firms. Does the minister tell me that if he had had Birkett buy these pistols he could not have saved the country at least one-half of the commission? I will go further. Is there a man within sound of my voice to-night, is there any man in Canada who has read the evidence, who does not believe that the Colt Revolver company paid a commission in some way or other to somebody? The vice-president of the Colt company swore that he made a present to Col. Allison, and said that it was for general business. Is there any man who believes that business is carried on in that way? Is there any man who believes that there was not a rake-off somewhere? There is something else the minister did not tell us this afternoon, when he was reading the evidence of Stone. He did not say that he was present when this trade was made.
Stone was not present.
Stone said the minister was present.
The minister made the deal; Allison had nothing to do with it.
He was present too.
Yes.

You always find Allison around. You will find Allison around in every transaction of this kind that has taken place in the United States since the day war was declared. Of course, the minister says that he is a saint, and that
[Sir Srm Hughes.)
everything is all right. We have no proof to the contrary, but we have a lot of suspicious circumstances. As I said before, Allison can come here and we will try and get the matter straightened out.
The minister has also been able to revolutionize the price of copper in the world to-day. He says that he has bad a smelting establishment erected in Canada and that this at once brought the price down. I have not bought any copper myself in the last three or four weeks, but I am buying copper quite frequently, and I know the price has been going up and up and up. The last I bought I paid 25 cents a pound for it. But I can discuss copper with the minister a little later on. He has copper on the brain , just now, and shells, and fuses, and things of that kind. Next Tuesday we shall have the pleasure of discussing shells, and fuses, and copper, and I know the minister will be present to discuss these things with us face to face. I will therefore reserve my remarks on copper, and fuses and shells. While I am on the subject, however, I might say that when it comes to letting a $22,000,000 contract for fuses, at an average price of $4.33J, we find Colonel Allison on the job again. Wherever you find the Militia Department doing business in the United States, there you find Colonel Allison. And another gentleman is usually found with him, one by the name of Harris. Probably the minister knows something about him. He has an interest in the shell business in Ontario. Like Colonel Allison, he is a great friend of his; he is always around when fuse contracts are being let.
He lives in New York.
Perhaps the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) could tell us something about this gentleman.
I know this man Harris is always around when contracts are being let.
Is there any harm in that?

I don't know. He is simply Allison's friend. The minister also told us this afternoon what a wonderful saving had been made on jjiotor trucks. I want to give my hon. friend credit where credit is due. I admit that the department bought motor trucks cheaper after April, 1915, than they did before, but how much cheaper I do not know. The minister gave us certain figures this afternoon, but you

E
f
know, Mr. Chairman, the minister's memory is bad when it comes to figures. I do not mean that he would mis-state a figure, but only that his memory is bad. However, the accounts will be brought down, and I presume we shall have a chance of verifying his figures. I should also like to know what 'has* become of this wizard in buying motor trucks, Col. Thomas. The minister referred to him this afternoon. This Col. Thomas appeared before the Public Accounts Committee over a period of three or four weeks last spring. He took all the credit to himself for reducing the price of motor trucks, and gave Allison none at all. Whenever we had a spare half-hour in the committee we used to put Col. Thomas on the stand, and he would tell us how he purchased the motor trucks. Then we would go on with our business, and when work became shy again, we would put Thomas on the stand and hear the story once more. But he seems to have disappeared altogether. He has not been seen around the city since October or November last. He may have gone to the front to look after motor trucks, or he may be in the United States buying more, or spending the winter in Florida with Allison and Morgan. Will the minister tell us where he. is?

Ool. Allison is the gentleman who first drew my attention to the plan by which the price could be reduced. He gave me the names of two, gentlemen who were experts in the business, and if, when I was speaking this afternoon, I omitted anything in this regard it was an act of omission, not of commission. I will tell the whole story. There is nothing being kept back at all. Colonel Allison got me in touch with Mr. Thomas, now Colonel Thomas-promotion comes rapidly when you do good work-and with a young gentleman by the name of Bucroft, who is the editor of some automobile journal in the United States, and one of the brightest young fellows it has been my privilege to meet. These three gentlemen thought out the plan, and I executed it. I am a little proud of that, because we saved Canada on these motor trucks the sum of $1,600,066. Thomas has since been sent over to England to consult with the British Government, and has been inspecting trucks at the front. He is returning to Canada at a very early date. His services have been recognized as very valuable both by this Government and the British Government.
The minister should tell him to take a little less credit to himself, and leave a little for Allison.
He was the expert.

Then Allison did not
play any part at all in the saving on these motor trucks?
Oh, yes, he did. He was the engineer of the show, Thomas was the expert, and I had the honour of being the driver.

There always seems to
be enough glory to go around. The minister is never shy on glory, he has a plentiful supply of it. They are all the finest chaps in the world as long as the money holds out. The minister has also referred to the Ross rifle, in practically the same terms he used a month ago. I am not here to defend or condemn the Ross rifle. I am free to admit that on many occasions in this Parliament during the last eight or ten years I have defended the policy of manufacturing rifles in Canada. I defend that policy to-day. I believe it is the proper policy, but I am surprised that in the conduct of his department, the minister has not gone further in connection with the manufacturing of war supplies in Canada than he has done. We have a big plant down in Quebec; I think my hon. friend referred to it as a blacksmith's shop. Well, it costs a lot of money to run that blacksmith's shop; the cost runs into hundreds of thousands of dollars a year; I refer to the arsenal. Is it not a most remarkable thing, Mr. Chairman, that we have been buying our war supplies, such as shrapnel shells and high explosives, though I do not believe we had any high explosives in Canada before the war comenced.
In Canada, we have made millions of high explosive shells. The Shell Committee-
I know more about the Shell Committee than my hon. friend thinks I do.
There were not high explosives made before the war.
No.

We will discuss the
Shell Committee next Tuesday, and probably without gloves. But to-day we are discussing the Militia Department, and the policy of manufacturing war supplies in Canada. I defended the Ross rifle propo-

sition some years ago, and I defend it today; but I want to say, in passing, that I only hope the Ross rifle is in the happy condition in which the minister claims it is. One would think, according to the description given by the minister this afternoon, that the Ross rifle was such a fine weapon that everybody in the Old Country had his eye on it, and that the soldiers had to sleep on it to keep other solders from stealing it, and substituting a Lee-Enfield, Of course I know that that was a figure of speech intended for the reporters.
I referred to sharp shooting.

Let us get down to the ordinary business, of Parliament for a little while. I have met four different soldiers within the last two months-I could give their names, but I do not wish to do so- two of them were sergeants and the other two privates. They were wounded soldiers who had returned from the front, and I discussed this matter with them. By a rather singular coincidence their statements agreed. They were partly commendatory of the Ross rifle, and- partly condemnatory. They all agreed that, for sniping, all the soldiers wanted the Ross rifle because it had the peep sight, and the men who were hidden had plenty of time in winch to shoot. But they said that for action or ordinary service the men would throw away their Ross rifles for a Lee-Enfield. I give that statement to the minister and to the House. I came to the conclusion that there must be something wrong with the Ross rifle as an ordinary weapon for trench, and field warfare, but if the minister can succeed in eliminating those difficulties, or, if. he has succeeded, as he says he has, I am glad.

I did not say there were difficulties. I stated that it had been discovered that the ammunition was at fault. The Canadian soldiers could not be expected to have confidence in their rifles when they were asked to answer those ten questions that were sent to them. The bad ammunition got mixed up with the good, and at the battle of St. Julien some of the rifles were found to be jamming. The soldiers who had not been accustomed to the Ross rifle might take it into their heads that the rifle .was at fault, but it was the fault of the ammunition. It is known now that the fault lay with the ammunition; the report of Field Marshal French showed that. The reports show that for many weeks

there has been nothing wrong except that some ammunition got mixed up again. My hon. friend *will remember that I read a letter from the inspector, a very capable officer, in which he stated that by some peculiar mischance a lot of bad ammunition got mixed up with the ammunition served out to the Canadians.

The minister told us on a former occasion that they had enlarged the chamber of the Ross rifle something like a two-thousandth part of an inch. Would that make any difference even if the soldiers got perfect ammunition? I am just giving the facts as I understand them. I know there has been a lot of dissatisfaction at the front, in England, and in Canada over the Ross rifle, but I sincerely hope that the minister has overcome the difficulties. If the difficulty was not with the rifle, of course the rifle cannot be blamed. I do not want to say anything here that would in any way be quoted as criticising or condemning the equipment of the Canadian army at the front.

I know my hon. friend does not. I am sure he will agree with me that when questions like those to which I have referred were distributed among the soldiers-and they were sent there with an object, whether by an enemy or not, I do not know-the men would not have a feeling of confidence in their arm, particularly on the eve of battle.

I agree with that, and I think the party responsible should be severely censured. I am very glad to learn that the fault in regard to the Ross rifle is with the ammunition and not with the rifle itself. But why is it, that in the three years during which my hon. friend was minister, prior to the outbreak of war, nothing was done in the way of manufacturing shells in Canada? We had an arsenal at Quebec. The minister made a statement which I could hardly credit, but I read it over in Hansard, and found that 1 had understood him correctly. He stated that they made only 75 shells a day at the arsenal, and that 75 per cent of these shells were no good. What is wrong with the outfit at Quebec anyway?

In the event of war taking place we felt that we would be in a better position to buy our shells, and we only made enough to meet ordinary requirements. Both our energies and our money went towards making Mark VII ammunition. The manufacture of shells was so

small that it would not count in the case of war.

That is the minister's explanation, and of course we must accept it, but to me it is a remarkable thing that the arsenal at Quebec, which costs, I am safe in saying, hundreds of thousands of dollars a year, was so utterly useless when the war broke out. The minister will remember that, prior to 1914, we on this side of the House called his attention on many occasions to the fact that his militia was not anything like what he said it was. We were compelled to point out that his principal business was building armouries and places of that kind; that he was not really building up the militia. While I do not want to cast any reflection on the Canadian militia, it would be very interesting now to get a return showing the number of men in the first contingent who had attended the annual drills five or six weeks prior to the time they were mobilized. However, that is a matter which we may bring up at another time.
There is one thing that must be impressed upon the minister, that musit be engraven upon his heart, and that is that if he is Minister of Militia after this war is over there will be a very different militia system in existence in Canada than that which prevailed, prior to the war. We used to listen to the bombastic speeches of the minister, in which he used to tell us about the 75,000 trained and equipped men whom he had ready to jump into the fray at a moment's notice. I think he has had cause to revise that opinion; but, fortunately, the yeomanry, the young men, the middle aged, men, and the old men of Canada, who did not belong to the militia, who were not under the special guidance of the minister, and did not know anything about his top-heavy militia department and system, jumped into the breach, and well it was that they did, because otherwise the minister would not have been able to read us the figures to-day, that will excite the pride of every Canadian, showing that there have been recruited 275,000 men in a year and a half. I do not know that the minister should take all the glory to himself. He had better distribute that glory around a bit.
Did I not try to do it to-day?

Yes, I admit that he did; he was very impartial in his distribution of the glory. If he 'had been as impartial
in his distribution of business favours as he was in throwing bouquets around the House we would not be criticising him.

I do not know how I can please my hon. friend. I was tackled by my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), who said: "This thing works one way altogether; no Tory in Portage la Prairie can get a contract; the Grits get them all." A 'friend from Brandon wrote to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and myself complaining that we had given the Grits of Brandon everything, and that nothing was given to the Tories at all. I get knocked on this side, I get knocked on that side, and all I can do is to settle down and keep going ahead on an even keel.
It is the same in Selkirk.
It is the same in Brock-ville.

That is internicine warfare, and I am not interested in it. The minister will have to settle that matter with his followers. But, to be serious, I would say that he has not got any more knocks than he deserves.
Prom both sides.
Yes, from both sides. I was very glad to hear the minister say this afternoon that he had got out of the patronage system as far as medical doctors were concerned.

I used the wrong term this afternoon, my deputy minister informs me, in speaking of the patronage list. The local officers have a purchasing list for small things in country towns, but I do not know anything about it. There is a purchasing list, for instance, in Portage la Prairie, Brandon, Pictou and other places. This purchasing list is sent to the local divisional officers, I believe.
This list must be all Tory then down in New Brunswick, because no Liberal has heard anything about it.
Anybody who has the line of goods desired can get on the list.

He can get on the list, but he will never be applied to, and therefore will not be enabled to sell anything. Being placed 'on the list is one thing, but being applied to and asked to sell goods is another thing. Will the minister say



that every man on the list will have a chance to supply the goods that he has to sell?

I do not know the first thing about the list. Such things are left to the local men. In Kingston, Brandon, Portage la Prairie, Brockville, and a hundred other places they have been tearing me limb from limb because I would not give them this business. Now, my hon. friend is tearing me limb from limb the other way.

That is a family fight. The minister says that he has no time to bother with these small things. All right; I agree that he is a busy man, but it would not take very much of the valuable time of the minister if he ordered his deputy to send out instructions that any man who has goods to sell should be put on the list and will have the right to tender.
That is the order now.
And that the lowest tender be accepted.
That is the rule which has invariably been followed.
Will the minister tell us that all over Canada that policy will be followed and that he will give instructions to that effect?

No, I cannot give instructions because I gave them long ago. Those are my instructions to the officers in various places. Not only that, but instead of placing the list pn the back door of a store, I have instructed them that the call for tenders shall be made public and that a list of the things required shall be sent to people able to supply them whether they are Liberals or Conservatives. That order has been in existence for years.
How long?

That was issued
before the war.

Then, I can
9 p.m. only say that the minister has been awfully deceived, that so.me-body has gone back on him or has double-crossed him, because, certainly down in my county no Liberals ever get a chance to tender on anything. There is no use in the minister talking about what he has done in this town or in that if they have not carried out his instructions. Every

gentleman sitting around me to-night can bear testimony to that. My hon. friend from Northumberlanad- (Mr. Loggie) was telling us this evening that in Chatham no Liberal could by any chance sell a loaf of bread.
Perhaps they do not deal in bread.

I hope my hon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) will pardon me if I do not reply to that sage remark at the present time. I want to have this thing thoroughly understood before leaving it; let us have no misunderstanding.

The deputy minister informs me that I was absolutely right in the statement I made and that at every place where troops are stationed the Army Service Corps invariably call for public tenders for these things.

I can tell the minister that that statement is not true. In Woodstock, New Brunswick, there have been 500 troops stationed since some time in December and there were no public tenders for supplies of any kind.
Are they fed by the Army Service Corps?

Certainly they are. Two good Tory firms were invited to tender for the groceries, they put their heads together and they decided that they would tender just exactly alike, and they put the tenders high enough. One of them double-crossed the other, he cut a little off the price and got the business. Nobody else got a chance to tender. The minister may have given instructions that Liberals might be given a chance to tender for groceries, meats and things of that sort, but there is somebody between him and the carrying out of his instructions and I do not think it is the deputy minister either. The whole thing gets down to local Tory patronage. When the minister interrupted me I was going to congratulate him. I was going to tell him that the arrangement he ha^ made whereby the commissioned officer of a corps can appoint a medical officer at any time he chooses to examine recruits is a move in the right direction. There may be some things that his Conservative friends may complain of in certain places; that is liable to happen. I imagine, from what he tells us that he does not take very much stock in some of these complaints. I think it is a move in the right direction because men

have been moved long distances to be examined, in many cases they have failed to pass the examination and it has been a cause of a great deal of inconvenience, and I believe, to some extent, has retarded recruiting.
And it has obviated the objection of keeping men waiting for weeks.

I commend my hon.
friend. I am glad to commend him when I can. Unfortunately, there are so few occasions when you can commend him and so many when you must criticise him. If the minister will carry out the promises he has made here lo-day and see that his ideals are carried oht in practice throughout the country, he will revolutionize Canada and will put the militia system on a different basis from what it has been on during the last four or five years; he will stimulate recruiting, and that ought to be the object of every patriotic citizen, regardless of ms politics. If the minister will do this, I shall be only too happy to come back here next session, if I am alive then, and commend him for doing so; but he has a big job on his hands; he is surrounded by a number of friends, I see them all around him; I know them all intimately.
Lots of friends.

Yes,, lots of friends, who will raise the biggest row that was ever raised in Canada if the minister endeavours to carry out these reforms. While the minister lias plenty of go and push in him, plenty of independence, it will take even more independence than he possesses to carry out the reforms he has promised. Conditions, however, are better than they were a year or so ago-the Lord knows they could not be any worse, and if there is a change at all, it will have to be for the better.
The department is not paying such high prices for some things.

No, they are buying
things much cheaper in some cases. Of course, there are many notable instances to the contrary. The are buying shells much cheaper.

Of course, they have
nothing to do with that.

The minister had all to do with that until the first day of December, 1915, and I must say there was a gradual reduction even before the minister
handed over the purchasing of shells to other people, so that we can give him credit for some improvement; but so far as buying goods out in the country is concerned, there has been no improvement at all. But if he carries out the great improvements he has promised and allows Liberals to be placed on the lists and allows Liberals in towns where troops are quartered to tender on the supply of provisions and so forth, he will make a great improvement and the country will not be called upon to pay as much as they have had to do in the past for carrying on the work of the department in connection with the war.
I was telling the Minister of Militia a little while ago that, as Colonel Allison is such a financial wizard that he has saved Canada and the Allies $50,000,000 on war purchases, the Minister of Finance should not fret and worry himself until he is getting grey-haired in his endeavour to raise money; he should send for Col. Allison and he will raise $50,000,000 by merely waving his hand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am very much obliged for the suggestion.
I will not say any more for the present, but there are a number of special items on which, of course, I will reserve the right to offer some mild criticism if I think it necessary.

In November last, some 275 men of the 76th Battalion were sent from Niagara to the town of Orillia to be kept there in the splendid armoury which has been erected in that town. Col. Caldwell, who is in charge of the regiment, asked the mayor of Orillia for the names of all the butchers, bakers and provision dealers so that he could get tenders from them, and the supplies were secured in that way without regard to politics whatever. I cannot speak of any other town than Orillia, but the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) tells me that 500 men were placed in the barracks in the town of Barrie and the provisioning was done in the same way, so that if the remarks of the hon. member as to provisioning of troops are as incorrect in New Brunswick as in the county of Simcoe, he would simply be laughed at if he went into that county.
He would not be laughed at in the province of New Brunswick.

We had 800 men of the 58th Battalion stationed at Brockville, and, when they came there, orders were sent by

the Minister of Militia that all supplies were to be publicly advertised for, and a Liberal in that town is now supplying all the groceries, vegetables, butter, eggs, etc. There are in BrockVille four other war contracts, two of which are held by Liberals and two by Conservatives. If the Minister of Militia has divided up his patronage in that way throughout the country, the Conservatives are not making much out of it.

I would like also to
say-
Next.

I would like to prove the utter fallacy-I will not use the word " falsity "-of the remarks of the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. A leading Liberal in Peterborough is providing 700 troops stationed there with provisions; and in order that there might be no criticism whatever of carelessness on my part in carrying out the instructions of the Militia Department, I inserted in the newspapers, including the Grit organ, a letter addressed to the Liberals, telling them that they could send their names to Major Hamilton of Kingston, who would put their names on the list and that they would be allowed to tender for whatever was required. It is a most shameful procedure to cast these reflections upon the Minister of Militia, especially at this juncture, and to say that such conditions are general throughout the country when, as a matter of fact, they are not by any means general, even if they are particular, and they might happen through carelessness or inadvertence.

I am sure the House will pardon me if I read this little dispatch from the front:
French midnight reports violent fighting resumed on Verdun front, especially Douaumont and Pepper Hill, where German infantry have been repulsed and decimated. British report recapture of 800 yards of trenches lost on February 14 at Ypres and Comines canal, and also taking of a German salient.

He was lucky then to
get it.

When such things as this
happen, I cannot understand how hon. gentlemen can expect the people to believe that the minister is conducting the affairs of his department without regard to politics.
