Last year, not in my own town but very near to it, contracts were let for the supply of hay and fodder for horses .as well as provisions for the troops, and Liberals were not given an opportunity to tender. I do not find so much fault with that. If these people would tell us that they are running this affair on patronage lines, it would not be so bad. But I certainly do object to any man standing up and telling me that the patronage system is not followed, when I know better, when I have seen it in my own town, and when I have seen the letters that show that the patronage system is followed in the purchase of even the smallest items for the Militia Department. In this contract for hay, not only were the Liberals not asked to tender, but the man who got the contract got it on condition, I am informed, that he he .should not even buy his hay from Liberals. These are things that I know. And does the Minister of Militia expect me to sit quiet and listen while he tells the House and the country that there is no patronage in his department? If he has been so fair to the Liberals in his own county, I congratulate him for it. But he thereby declares for a principle, and that principle should be carried out elsewhere. Though that may be the case in his own county, it is not true of my county, nor of the province of New Brunswick, and from what I hear from other hon. gentlemen on this side, it is not true in other parts of the Dominion, especially the Maritime Provinces. If the minister has had a change of heart, and intends

in future to conduct his department on the lines he says, I am sure the country will be glad of it. As has been reiterated in this House, if there ever was a time when every dollar of the public funds should be rigidly safeguarded and honestly and wisely expended, this is that time. If the Minister of Militia has seen the error of his ways and intends in future to give every person that can do so an opportunity to supply goods, I congratulate him. But he can hardly blame us for taking his statement with a grain of salt when w<j know how he has epred in the past. I think the time has come when hon. members who know that these things are taking place should tell the people the facts as to their own ridings; and I believe that what is true of my constituency is true of most other constituencies in Canada.

It Is refreshing to hear hon. gentlemen opposite criticising the Government for its purchases in connection with this war. This is not the only war in which Canada has indulged; we had the Boer war when the Liberal party was in power, and perhaps hon. gentleman opposite could tell the House how many Conservatives participated in the supplying of the troops then.

I could tell the hon.
gentleman some in New Brunswick.

Very few, I am sure. It is well known that for years, during the reign of the Liberal party, they built up - such a system of patronage in connection with the Militia Department that, when this war took place, not a man could make even a pair of trousers for the troops unless he was a Liberal. Practically all the supplies for the first contingent in the (present war were furnished by Liberals. My hon. friend (Mr. Copp) talks about his own county and about New Brunswick. Well, I come from the West-the West which has furnished two men for every one furnished elsewhere in Canada-and I want to tell the hon. gentleman a few facts. In the city of Winnipeg we have ten battalions; in the West we have about fifteen battalions. I think I know what is going on in the West, and I believe that there is not .an hon. member of this House who comes from the West who will make with regard to his constituency a similar statement to that made by the hon. gentleman. The 108th battalion is stationed at my own town of Selkirk. The barracks was obtained from a Liberal,
member of the local legislature. Every dollar of the money spent in fitting up the
barracks went to improve his property. There were other places that we could have got, but there was no intention of making a party question out oif it. I often wonder, as I hear such criticisms as that to which we have listened to-day, whether the party, as a party, has been justified in being as fair as it has been to the Liberals, for they get no credit for it. 'In connection with supplies for the 108th battalion, tenders were invited, and the contract went to one of the strongest Liberals in Selkirk, a man who, to my knowledge, never cast a Conservative vote. 'Tenders were received from two or three Liberals and from two Conservatives. No, attempt was made to limit the opportunity to tender to the Conservatives of that district. Take the commanding officers in Manitoba to-day. I believe there are as many Liberals as Conservatives, if not more. And these men have a good deal to do with guiding affairs, so far as patronage is concerned. I do not believe that in the choice of officers in the West, politics has cut any figure. In my own battalion, I have never asked a man where he stood politically. Some of my majors, captains and lieutenants are Liberals. I never asked what their politics were; I was looking for efficiency, and I am sure that is what every commanding officer in the West 'has been doing. I believe that the same thing applies all over Canada. I hold no brief for the minister or for his department; if they have made mistakes- they are able to defend themselves. It would be strange if they had succeeded in spending the large amount of money that has been spent without making some mistakes, but I say that the criticism which has been made with regard to patronage is unfair and unfounded so far as Western Canad,a is concerned.

I thought that some hon. gentleman on the other side of the House would come to the rescue of the Minister of Militia. In doing so the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has admitted exactly what we-diave been charging, because he attempts to defend the minister and the department by saying that the Liberal party did the same thing when they were in power.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friends may say "oh," but that is the first argument that thq hon. gentleman offered in answer to the statements made on this side of the House. He talked about what the Liberal party did at the time of the Boer war.
This party is not doing the same, though.

My bon. friend did not say that before he sat down. He says that we on this side of the House are not conducting ourselves in a proper and patriotic manner, because, forsooth, we have the temerity to offer criticism in regard to the conduct of the Government respecting certain public [DOT]matters. Is it out of place for hon. gentlemen on this side of the House to make statements as to how affairs are conducted in their own particular constituencies and provinces? The hon. member for -Selkirk took exactly the same ground. The arguments that my hon. friend has made prove that the charges we have advanced are absolutely well founded. He says they are not true in respect of his particular constituency, and he cites proof of this, so far as the province of Manitoba and the city of Winnipeg are concerned, My hon. friend seeks to place himself upon a higher pedestal than that occupied by his colleagues on the opposite side of the House. He says that in the province of Manitoba and in his constituency where he has the patronage, the criticism made by hon. gentlemen on this side has no application. I do not controvert the hon. gentleman's assertion, but I do say that if these charges are not true in the province of Manitoba or in his constituency, they are true in other constituencies. It has been proved that they are true, and I can show in black and white that they are true. My hon. friend says that these things have not been done in his constituency, and, in the next breath, he adds that it is wonderful that the hon. minister did not make more mistakes than he has made. The minister has made many mistakes, Mr. Chairman. I am not here to question my hon. friend's veracity, -and, if he has been fair to his constituents in the statement which he has made, I commend and congratulate him for being able to rise above the methods of a party that have traded down to the very last ditch in the matter of patronage and graft in connection with the public affairs of this country. I can say to him, however, that in the great majority of constituencies in Canada they have not 'been able to rise to that high level that my hon. friend claims to have attained in respect of the patronage in his own county.	[DOT]

I am sure it is a great shock to the hon. member for Peel to hear it asfMr. Copp.]
serted over and over again that there is at the present time a patronage list in the Department of Militia and Defence. I remember during the years that the member for Peel sat in Opposition how very strong he was on the subject of patronage lists. The very thought of there being a patronage list in existence for any purpose whatever, in respect even of the most trifling services br the most trifling purchases, was enough to cause him to manifest as much of an ecstacy of passion as his placid temperament is capable of. Even with respect to the advertisements published from time to time in the newspapers of the country, he used to ask the minister day after day whether or not this patronage was accorded by tender. It was disclosed in the Public Accounts Committee last year, and yesterday as well, that there is a patronage list in the Militia Department. If hon. gentlemen will turn to the evidence given in the Public Accounts Committee a year ago, they will find there the statement, made by the present purchasing agent of the Department of Militia and Defence, that there is at the present time a patronage list in that department, containing about 8,000 names. This gentleman also stated that there was a small patronage list previous to 1896, and that it had grown from very small proportions in 1911 to 8,000 at the present time. The same courteous and efficient officer was examined in the Public Accounts Committee yesterday, and he gave similar testimony.
The hon. member for Selkirk endeavoured to score a point against the late Government in respect of expenditures made during the Boer war. No comparison whatever can be made with the circumstances under which the late Government carried on its very moderate part in the Boer war and the magnitude of the interests which are in the hands of the present Minister of Militia and Defence in respect of the present conflict. The total expenditure in respect of the Boer war for supplies and equipment of troops in Canada was defrayed by the British Government.^ The taxpayers of Canada were under no obligation to provide the money necessary to defray the expenses of our participation in that war. To-d,ay, however, the taxpayers of Canada are deeply concerned in the expenditures of the Government in connection with the present war. Again, the services rendered by the Canadian Government at the itime of the Boer war in respect of the* number of men recruited and equipped at

that time were insignificant compared with the campaign for men that has been going on in ths country during the last two years. Further, whereas the number of Canadians who took part in the South African war was only a few thousand, I have it upon the authority of the right hon. Prime Minister himself that he hopes to see 500,000 Canadians in the field in the course of the present year. This will involve an enormous expenditure of money- an expenditure which must be defrayed by the taxpayers of Canada. Every city, town, hamlet, and agricultural community in the whole of Canada is concerned in the manner in which our participation in the war is carried out, and how that participation is to be financed. In every section of Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, appeals are being made at the present time for recruits. Every taxpayer, every father of a family, be he Liberal or Conservative, is.asked to permit his boys who are under age to join the colours; sons of these parents, irrespective of politics, are being asked to give their services to King and country. They are all responding magnificently to the call. There is no difference of opinion as to what Canada's duty is. The only distinction that has prevailed is that which has been made by the Minister of Militia and Defence in 'his department in the matter of patronage. While it is the privilege of the sons of Lib-, erals to take their places in the trenches and to suffer and die for the Empire, it is the privilege only of Conservatives to enjoy the patronage which this enormous expenditure involves.
There is another point to which I wish to direct the attention of the hon. member for Selkirk, with respect to. the difference between the Boer war and the present war. We do know that the late Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) was attacked time and again on the floor of this House in respect of the administration of his department with reference to the part Canada took in the Boer war. But it is a fact that the most eloquent, forceful and strenuous defender of the late Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) was the present Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes). We do know that time and again when members supporting the then Opposition challenged the conduct of the then Minister of Militia in respect of his management of Canada's share in the Boer war, the first man upon his feet to defend Sir Frederick Borden was the present Minister of Militia. Has any such thing happened during this discussion?
From the temper of hon. gentlemen sitting on these benches, I do not think there is much danger of any gentleman rising in his place to defend the minister.
If the late minister was here he might.

If he were here he would do the right thing, and I question whether he would consider it the right thing to defend the Minister of Militia to-night. I was going on to speak of the recruiting campaign that is going on throughout this Dominion. I have very much pleasure in being able to say that there is no part of the Dominion that in the last few days has contributed more men to the colours than the province of Nova Scotia. I saw in the Montreal Star last night that in two days 1,200 recruits in Nova Scotia had enlisted and taken their places at the different stations where training is going on. The province of Nova Scotia, I venture to say, in proportion to its population, will contribute as much as any other province in the Dominion, and perhaps more. Nova Scotia is a small province comparatively speaking. Her population is less than 500,000 and in order to get 1,200 recruits in two days, and the 13,000 recruits who have come to the colours in the province of Nova Scotia in the last year and a half it was necessary to appeal to men of all classes and of all political parties, and men of all classes and of all political parties have come readily to the colours. I repeat what I have said before, now that the minister is in his place, that the only attempt that has been made to create any political division in this recruiting campaign has been made by the Department of Militia and Defence, which persists iif drawing the party line in respect to patronage. In the county of Cape Breton a large number of young men have enlisted and gone to the front. They have borne their part well. There are families in Cape Breton that have con tributed not only one, or two, or three, but in some instances four sons to the various Canadian regiments. A very considerable sum of money has been expended in the city of Sydney in respect of the training of soldiers and the maintenance of interned aliens. But I venture to say that up to the present-unless it was by some accident that can not be accounted for-not a single dollar of the large sum of money that has been spent by this Government in the county of Cape Breton has ever reached the coffers of a Liberal. Why the statement the Minister of Militia made to-

night, if it were intended to apply to patronage as it has been distributed in the county of Cape Breton would be laughed at by every sane man in the county. And not only that, but there has been partisanship in the selection of recruiting officers. Last year I remember a very active recruiting campaign was carried on in the Island of Cape Breton. I attended a recruiting meeting which was addressed by a man in civilian clothes. This man had not received any appointment. As a matter of fact the recommendation that he be appointed a recruiting officer was turned down by the Department of Militia and Defence. That man made a speech that night which was the most effective recruiting speech I have heard since the war began. He had only one son, and this young man was among the first to join the colours from the island of Cape Breton. He had been for many months in the trenches and had borne his part well and bravely, and his father had, therefore, warrant to come before the young men of the province of Nova Scotia and ask them to come forward, and to do what his only son had done and what he was proud his only son was willing to do. After the meeting I asked this gentleman if he had been appointed a recruiting officer. He said: No, I am not a recruiting officer; in view of the service I am giving the department and the island of Cape Breton in addressing recruiting meetings it was suggested that I be appointed a recruiting officer, but the gentleman who spoke in my behalf was told that the only way I could be appointed would be upon a recommendation to that effect from the Tory candidate of the riding. Now, Mr. Speaker, this man and the Tory candidate do not happen to be on very good terms, consequently the man did not receive the appointment. But that did not cool his ardour. Wherever he happened to be in the performance of his duty, if there was a recruiting meeting going on he would be the first man there and he always made the most effective recruiting speech of the meeting. During the last couple of weeks I understand that he has been appointed a recruiting officer. Not, however, by the Minister of Militia, but by the chief recruiting officer for the province. He had heard the success this man had had in getting recruits and he came to him and asked if he would continue his services. The chief recruiting officer said: I have no authority to appoint 
you but I will take the responsibility myself. The man accepted this quasi appointment, and at the present time he is one of the most active and successful recruiting officers in the province of Nova Scotia.
There is one other matter I desire to refer to and that is with respect to the appointment of medical officers. There is a medical man in the province of Nova Scotia who is well known to every member of this House. He has had many years of experience in his profession. His practice has been most successful. I refer to Dr. J. B. Black, of the county of Hants, formerly an honoured member of Parliament. Now Dr. Black was anxious to do his bit in this war. While he is a man up in years he is still active in the practice of his profession, and he felt that the obligation rested upon him to do what in him lay towards the alleviation of the sufferings of Canadian soldiers wounded in the war. He addressed a letter to General G. Carlton Jones, Surgeon General, who is at present in England, and I have here General Jones' reply:
London, W.C., 10th December, 1915.
Dear Doctor Black,-I am very glad indeed to hear from you, but I am sorry to say that it does not lie within my power to cable for you to come over here, but if you can arrange it with Ottawa, I can easily place you for service in England, and would be glad to have your professional services.
We are at present short of medical officers, and we would be only too pleased if you could come and help us.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) G. C. Jones,
Surgeon-General,
Director of Medical Services, Canadian Contingents.
Doctor J. B. Black,
Windsor, Nova Scotia,
Canada.
Upon receipt of this letter, Dr. Black wrote the following letter to Mr. E. M. Macdonald, M.P.:
Windsor, N.S., December 29, 1915.
E. M. Macdonald, M.P.,
Pictou, N.S.
My dear Macdonald,-I have been very anxious for some time to do some part of a citizen's duty in this war and more particularly to do some part in caring for our wounded Canadian soldiers.
At the suggestion of Dr. John Stewart of Halifax (Colonel Stewart of the Dalhousie Unit) I wrote direct to Surgeon General G. Carlton Jones, London, of the Canadian Forces. A copy of his answer I enclose. Now why I am writing you is,-I do not feel that General Sir Sam Hughes would receive graciously an application for a commission in the Army Medical Department from me personally, but I have understood that party politics has not

clouded a friendly admiration of each other by you and General Hughes, so I am writing you to ask if you will do the good office of applying for me.
As near as I can analyse my motives I am not selfish in this matter. I am not worrying about pay for I have sufficient private income to meet my needs; besides X have all the practice here that I want to do. It is not a desire for a trip abroad, for I have done Europe more than once, as well as looking over India, China and Japan besides. My wander-lust is fully satis-fled. Further, I have had most of the honours that my medical brethren in Canada can give me. I have been president of our Colchester-Hants Medical Association, president of the Nova Scotia Medical Association, and vice-president of the Canadian Medical Association, and other honours. To close a very busy life I would, above all things, desire to give myself for service to our wounded who have fought for the saving of the Empire; and from Surgeon General Jones' letter, there is work for me in England.
Yours very truly,
(Signed) J. B. Black.
The result of this correspondence, and of this offer on the part of Dr. Black, was that he received no appointment from the minister. I would like to get from the hon. minister a statement as to whether or not Dr. Black's offer reached him, and if it did reach him, why some appointment of the kind asked for has not been given him.

Does Dr. Black
claim that he made any application to the Department of Militia and Defence?
He claims to have made an application through the hon. member for Pictou to the hon. minister.
I do not remember anything about it.

I have the minister's letter
here; I will not read it to the committee, but will pass it over to him.
I have no objection to that letter being read.

If the hon. minister has no objection, and in order to complete the correspondence, I shall put the letter on Hansard :
. Minister's Office,
. Ottawa, January 10, 1916.
Private.
Dear Mr. Macdonald:
I have much pleasure in acknowledging receipt of your letter of the 30th ultimo, enclosing correspondence from Dr. Black, relative to his desire to be of service in connection with this terrible war.
In reply I beg to advise you that there is a very simple remedy in connection with Dr. Black's case. If he will apologize for what he
has done I will be pleased to do what I can for him.	-
With kind regards,
Faithfully,
(Sgd.) Sam Hughes.
Shame!

Now we have the secret of the minister's refusal to entertain the offer of Dr. Black to serve in this war. He asks for an apology for some fancied offence that Dr. Black has committed. I think the hon. minister should recognize that it was in his capacity as Minister of Militia and Defence, and in that capacity only, that he was approached by Dr. Black for this appointment. Whatever personal pique may exist on the part of the minister, I should have thought that he was too big a man to allow it to influence his judgment in a matter of this kind.
You do not know him.

That remains to be seen. I refuse to believe that the hon. minister is not a big enough man to overcome whatever personal ill will he has towards Dr. Black, and I trust that the minister will be equal to the occasion, and accede to the patriotic request made by Dr. Black that he' be given an opportunity to contribute his share of service in this war.

Dr. Black seems to have taken a very peculiar line. He applies first to a gentleman in England, and then to a gentleman in Nova Scotia. It would have been a simple matter for him to have applied to the military authorities in Halifax. He is much over the military age, and I may say that we have refused the services of many a good Tory for that reason. Being an old Parliamentarian, Dr. Black should have known that he had a very simple remedy. When I knew of his application, I took the matter up with the proper officers and it was decided that he should comply with the very simple procedure which he will understand. If he complies with that procedure I will remove any objections which I might urge to his being appointed.

Dr. Black wrote to Surgeon-General Jones to know if there was any position in which he could be useful. The hon. minister could not possibly know that. I think Dr. Black took the proper course in writing to Surgeon-General Jones in England, because unless that officer found that there was some position which Dr.

Black could fill, it would have been useless for Dr. Black to have applied to the minister. In regard to Dr. Black's age, every member who recollects him will remember that he was one of the most active members in this House. I desire to say further to the minister that if Dr. Black is oyer age, he is no more so than Colonel John Stewart, who was sent overseas in charge of the Dalhousie unit. In all the circumstances, I hope the minister will withdraw any objections he may have had, and that Dr. Black will be privileged to place his services at the disposal of the medical staff.

I understand that Dr. Stewart is a very estimable gentleman, and I believe that Dr. Black is also; but Dr. Stewart was selected by the officers of his unit. The officers were given the opportunity to select their own medical officer, and they selected Dr. Stewart. If they had selected Dr. Black, he would have been appointed.

When the statement is mad'fe in this committee by the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence that the affairs of his department are managed without any partisanship, or without any partisan bias, I do not think it would be fair for any member who knows the facts and the practice, locally at all events, to be different altogether, to allow the|Canadian people to suppose that things are as , the minister represents them to be. It is indeed a pity that this country has arrived at a stage when, whether wittingly or hot, ministers of the Crown stand up in this House and make statements, possibly believing them to be true, that are absolutely wide of the mark. The people of this country have >a right to suppose that when a minister representing the Crown stands up and makes a statement [DOT]of fact, he knows what he is talking about, and that representing his King and country honestly and truthfully and properly the condition of affairs is as he represents them to be.
I have no fault to find with the ordinary patronage practice. If there is a big contract which the statute requires to go out to tender in the ordinary condition of things, I insist that it should go out to tender. Under the ordinary conditions which prevailed before the war, if there were cases in which the interests of the country could be fairly well protected by ^the discretion of officers, .and they ' gave the preference to the 'friends of ithe .Government, I have no fault to find. But that was when they were spending the ordinary

revenues along ordinary lines. That was the practice when I was in this House supporting the Government. When I had the patronage in the county which I represent I had no fault to find with it, and I am not hypocritical enough to find fault with the Conservative party for doing what we did ourselves. But I do find fault with the practice that exists to-day when conditions are entirely different. There was no war in our time. To-day we are asking every man in this country to pay money towards carrying on the war; we tax him heavily for the purposes of the war.
They go to him for contributions to the Patriotic and other funds, and the money is expended by the ministers of a Tory Government, or by their officials. There is no party line drawn in the collecting of the money, they collect from Grit and Tory alike, and the Grit boys are just as able and patriotic and courageous in the trenches as the Tories, and when there is any profit, or preference, or emolument, to be bestowed, it should be divided equally amongst those who are entitled to it. If that is not done, the minister should have the courage to say boldly: No, we are conducting this thing along party lines; we have done it in the past and we are going to do it in the future. There would be some manly courage in that, and the people would at all events know that they were doing it on party lines and that they were not trying [DOT] to conceal it. But, we heard to-night the absolutely unfounded statement that the minister did not know about politics entering into the matter at all, that there was no preference in the management of the department, no patronage list, and that everything was going splendidly and beautiful. It has been pointed out by my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp), and my hon. friend from. Richmond (Mr. Kyte), that it was only yesterday that we had sworn evidence in the iCommittee on Public Accounts to the contrary. In that committee one of the officials of the department went on the stand and swore that this patronage list existed, that only the names of Tories were on it, and that everything from the smallest to the biggest had to come to the department through that list. That is sworn testimony, and I believe it to be true, notwithstanding what the minister says to the contrary.
Now, I desire to say a word as to Cape Breton and Victoria. As far as Victoria is concerned, there has been assemblage of troops in that county since the war broke out, and we are not complaining of patron-

age, because there was no patronage there. But there was a large body of men at North Sydney and a battery at Sydney Mines which came from Prince Edward Island. They were there for eight or nine months. Large bodies of troops were recruited at both these points. I venture to tell the minister that never did a fifty cent piece reach the pocket of a Liberal in Sydney or Sydney Mines. The only instance in North Cape Breton in which a Liberal received anything at all was when a man, who was building a barracks at Sydney Mines, wanted some nails; he went into a store kept by a Liberal and bought sixty cents worth. About an hour afterwards he came back and dumped the nails on the counter, saying: I am not allowed to buy these nails fropa you; I told the man 10 p.m. who is i,n charge of the patronage that I had bought the nails from you and he stated that 'be would not vouch for them; here are your nails, I have brought them back. That is a case in point and everything else has been done in the same way. A Liberal in the county of Cape Breton is not given a blank tender. They scorn the idea of giving him a paper on which to put a figure by way of tender, and yet, in the face of that, the minister *comes here and says that everything is done in the highest, the loftiest, and most patriotic way. He stands up like a bronze god and says that be knows nothing about it. . That is another trick of the department. When we have $73,000 in cash sent down to the county of Kings, NjS., to buy glue pot horses, the Minister of Militia gathers his angelic wings around him and says: I d,id not appoint the man, I did not furnish the cash and I know nothing about it. I suppose we have to believe him, at .all events, in the Parliamentary sense. The right lion, the Prime Minister (Sir Kobert Borden) told us on the 15th of April last that it was a boy who had undertaken to buy these horses without any business experience, and that he should never have undertaken the job. I would call the attention of the business men on the other side of the House to the capacity of the *Government which they support, as disclosed by this extraordinary transaction. A boy, without business experience, who, according to the Prime Minister, should never have undertaken the job, is able to go into the Militia Department, get $73,-*000 in cash, put it in 'his pocket, and run to the country_with it, and yet the minister knows nothing about it. That is the way the business of the country is conducted. I want the people of Canada to know that a boy, according to the Prime Minister, without any business experience, and who never should have undertaken the job, was entrusted with this money. I am only repeating what the Prime Minister said, I am not expressing any opinion of my own, or of Mr. Foster. How he got that money the minister does not know because he tells us he knows nothing about it. If anybody can go into the Militia Department and get money, we ought to know it, so that some of us might be able to get some of the money lying around loose there. The people of the country want to know something about the business methods of a Government under which this kind of thing can happen. The money of the Government was taken in that loose way and horses that could be bought for two drakes and a duck were returned to the department.	*
There is another matter that I think should be cleared up before these Estimates are put through. We heard the speech of the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. C'urrie) the other day and it disclosed a most extraordinary condition of things. He said that the Canadian boys had been hired out in England to build railways and huts for some. English contractor or other at 25 cents a day, and that they never got anything out of it except that trifling amount. I call upon the minister to tell the Canadian people, to tell the mothers and fathers of the young men who were sent to the front, as they thought, to fight, for their country, to be trained a& soldiers and to be instructed in the art of war, why it was that they were put to work to build huts and to become the ordinary navvies of an English contractor at 25 cents a day. That is a statement made by an officer of the Canadian Expeditionary Force -to this House. So far it has not been contradicted or explained. As a matter of fact, in the interest of good government and the proper handling of the affairs of this country, the people want to know what has become of the money. Is this another piece of graft, is it collusion between some authority who has control of these men and the English contractor, by which able-bodied men were made to work for 25 cents a day, the balance of the wages going somewhere else -than into the treasury of Canada or that of the British Government? In conclusion let me say that whatever the minister may say about the counties iu

Manitoba, Ontario, and other provinces, the patronage in my county could not be closer to the lines of party patronage and politics than it is at present, because I have given the only sample where a Liberal sold anything or anything was bought from a Liberal, and that was 60 cents worth of nails, and they were returned.

The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) has referred to the soldiers working in England. That was at a time when huts were very much needed because the huts put up by the war office proved very ineffective owing to the rainy weather. It was in connection witn that work that the soldiers were asked to turn in and build those huts. My information at the time, and since then was that it war, purely voluntary work and that they were given this additional pay as a bonus by the British Government, and that there was no objection on the part of the men. I objected to the men being taken away to do this work because of bad weither or anything else, and the work was stopped.
Mr. J J. HUGHES: The other day Col. Currie stated that the contractor charged $1.10 a day and that he paid the men only 25 cents a day.	_
No.
That was the statement that was made.

I am afraid there must be some misunderstanding. I have had some considerable difficulty in understanding the political situation in certain spots here and there throughout the Dominion and let me say in all frankness that parts of Nova Scotia are included in that. Politicians on both sides from these districts seem to be very particular about the patronage lists, and I think it would take a Philadelphia lawyer to keep track of these lists. But our orders are explicit and in the early period of the war I learned from time to time that troops have been quartered in certain places in such a hurry that there was no opportunity of calling for tenders, and in such cases recourse was had to the old patronage lists. Possibly that is how some of these grievances occurred, but I know that practically throughout the whole of the Dominion the proper custom was followed.

I have just received a telegram stating that a new battery of ar-

tillery has been ordered, to my native town of Woodstock. That means about 150 men and 70 horses. Will the minister give me his pledge to-night that Liberal storekeepers, merchants, men who can supply forage and other provisions will have an opportunity of tendering for the supplies for these troops on the same basis as the Tories? I want to put the minister to the test.
I am willing to be put to any test. The order has gone and will be carried out.
And Liberals will have an opportunity of tendering?
Public tenders will be called for in every place where troops are quartered. I want that distinctly un, derstooa.

In regard to the Canadian troops receiving twenty-five cents a day for their work in building the huts, I understood that that was in addition to the pay which they received from the Canadian Government?
Yes.

Col. Currie, however,
stated that had the men been working for the British Government there would have been no trouble, but his charge, was that he had discovered, later on that these men were working for a contractor, and not for the British Government, and that the contractor paid the men only twenty-five cents a day, thus making a large profit on their labour, and Col. Currie thought it was the duty of the Canadian Government to see that these men were fully paid* by the British Government.
I requested Gen. Carson to take the matter up immediately and have it adjusted in that way, or else we_would, hold the British Government responsible, charging them $1.10 a day for our men.

There is being raised
on the south side of the river in the constituency of Strathcona the 151st Battalion under Lieutenant Colonel Arnott. The senior major is Major Grant and the junior major is Major Lowrie from Lloydminster.
I am informed on the highest authority that these officers have no say whatever as to the selection of their captains and lieutenants, and that every one 'of these men must first of all receive a recommendation

from Mr. Crawford, the local member for South Edmonton.	.
He has no more to do with it than a child has. If I find that he has, he will not have it any longer.

He did have something to do with it. The colonel was not allowed to entertain any request for a commission in that regiment without a recommendation as to the character of the applicant by this Mr. Crawford or a Mr. Aldridge, the Conservative candidate for Strathcona.
He is a Methodist clergyman, perhaps the man was getting a clergyman's certificate.

Such a condition as this is not at all fair to the recruiting officers in the constituency of Strathcona because, without showing any undue pride, I may say that we in the northern part of Alberta -can point with pride to the large number of soldiers who have been recruited in the Edmonton district in particular. I know for a fact that this practice has been going on, although the minister may- not know anything about it, during the raising of the last four or five battalions in the city of Edmonton, I am informed on good authority that no subaltern can get a commission either in the 138th, or in the old battalions of the 51st and the 66th, without first of all getting a recommendation from Mr. Percy Abbott, one of the dispensers of patronage in Edmonton.
These are conditions that should be righted, and that is why I call the attention of the minister to them. These things were current talk on the streets of Edmonton when I left, and I have no reason to believe that conditions have changed since then. I know for a fact that men had to get that certificate. I am not saying that no one except Conservatives could get an appointment, for that would not be in good taste, nor would it show good judgment on the part of any candidate. But the fact remains that every man had to get that certificate. In connection with that, I have a letter and some telegrams from Major Thibaudeau, objecting to the minister not allowing him to raise a French-Canadian battalion in the district of Edmonton. I am not prepared to say whether he is justified in attempting to raise a French-Canadian battalion or not, but I desire to read the telegrams that have passed:
Edmonton, Alberta, February 21. General Sir Sam Hughes.
Minister of Militia,
Ottawa.
Are you going to accept offer to raise from Alberta and Saskatchewan Battalion French Canadians. Freely discussed here that report from G.O.C. District is that it is impossible and impracticable. Notwithstanding I can do it, if no undue interference is placed in my way. Tour department has had two months to consider offer and only fair I should receive answer whether my offer to be accepted or not.
DeBlois Thibaudeau.
On the 22nd of February the hon. gentleman sent the following characteristic reply:
*	Ottawa, Ont., February 22, 1916.
Major DeBlois Thibaudeau,'
Edmonton.
Wire received. Have made inquiries. First, find you are not reported upon favourable for command. Second, there are not enough French Canadians to maintain a company mucn less a battalion in the area spoken of. Third, the great majority of them prefer mixing with English speaking people and are loyally joining other battalions. Fourth, there are not sufficient in the whole northwest of Canada to maintain corps and all details.
Sam Hughes.
I have a statement here of the number of Freneh-Canadians in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, taken from the census returns of 1911. These show that in the province of Alberta there aTe 19,825 Freneh-Canadians. In the province of Saskatchewan there are 23,251; a total of over 40,000 in the provinces.
That includes halfbreeds.

It may, but I do not think the proportion of half-breeds would be very great at the present time, and I do not suppose that the hion. minister would object to French-Canadian halfbreeds joining the French-Canadian battalion.
They talk of raising two or three French-Canadian halbbreed regiments.
Has the hon. minister given authority.
For two.
In the West?
Yes.
In Alberta?
I will give full details as soon as I have heard from the office in the West.

I am merely bringing this Alberta preposition to the minister's attention. I am not sufficiently conversant with the details to know whether the minister is justified in sending this telegram or not, but in my own constituency there are 2,300 French Canadians.
Pardon me, there is nothing of the kind; there may be that number including half-breeds.
I am mistaken to this extent, that the exact number is 2,064.
I have gone over it a good many times.

I wish to put myself right with that class of our people, and the statement made by the minister in this telegram, that there are not enough French Canadians in the West to form a company, much less a regiment, is absolutely beside the truth.

As the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) comes from the West, and it might be supposed that in the matter of patronage he speaks for the whole West, I would like to say a few w ords in regard to what goes on especially in the constituency I have the honour to represent. The hon. member for Selkirk, I think, must have been asleep for the last year or two, if he has found no patronage in the vicinity of Selkirk. I am afraid he occupies a somewhat similar position with reference to the question of patronage as he occupies with reference to the question of the St. Peter's Indian reserve. It is only within the last six months or so that he has awakened to the fact that the people of Selkirk did not approve of his position.
They paid $50,000 for the land you gave away.

I will leave that for the hon. gentleman's constituents to settle with him, and, judging from the newspapers, the hon. gentleman will have a pretty hard task. However, as to the party patronage, it may be possible that the leopard has changed his spots in the vicinity of Selkirk, although I am afraid that the fact is that the hon. member simply does not know what is going on around him. But as to the city of Regina, from which I come, and also Moosejaw, Saskatoon and Prince Albert, I can say that party patronage never ran rife-especially in Regina-as it has since this war began. I do not blame the

minister altogether for this state of affairs.
I believe he is sincere when he says he tries to put down patronage in connection with his department. But throughout the length and breadth of Saskatchewan, they have got away from the minister. The hon. gentleman tells us that tenders are publicly called for, or, at least, that his instructions have been that they should be called for. We know that the Army Service Corps purchases the supplies for the soldiers at the points where they are stationed. Public tenders have not been asked for in Regina since the 4th of August, 1914, when the war broke out. Not a solitary advertisement, I think, has appeared in the press of either party calling for tenders for supplies. I am informed that the' same is true of the other cities of which I have spoken. The hon. minister speaks of a purchasing list.
I understand that he means the general purchasing list, and not a purchasing list for each constituency.	.

Before we handed over the work to the War Purchasing Department, our orders were exactly as I have stated. I think that in one or two cases, where they had no time to get the army service corps ready, they called for a purchasing list from the mayor of the town- as occurred in the case referred to by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett).
I know what our orders were, and we carried them out as far as we could. If any . officers are found deviating from it, they would be given to understand that they must obey orders.
I do not understand that. Was there a general purchasing list in the department?
No, but each locality has its own purchasing list, I understand. It is not my department, but the War Purchasing Department.
Is there a purchasing list in the department for the city of Regina?
Not in our department; there is in the office in Winnipeg, I presume. I suppose they wire the Mayor of Regina, or something like that.

They do not wire from
there, I can tell the hon. minister that. However, we get back to this position: there is a purchasing list for each constituency.

Grits and Tories
alike.

I fail to see the difference between a purchasing list and a patronage

list. I could have shown the minister a good deal of correspondence last session in respect to purchases in that portion of the country. Business men in the city of Regina who contribute hundreds of dollars to patriotic funds could not get one dollar's worth of business from the Militia Department, or from the Army Service Corps, which represents the Militia Department in Regina: they were not even asked to tender. As I have already stated, tenders were never called for in the newspapers.

They are never
called for in the newspapers; they are called for by means of posters,

That is something new to me. My information is that no advertisement by poster or in the newspapers was ever published since the war began, in or around the cities of Regina, Moosejaw, Prince Albert or Saskatoon, calling for tenders for war supplies.
I do not undertake to say that the hon. member is in error, but I do undertake to say that posters have been put up.

I should not like to question the hon. minister's information, but I live in that part of the country, and I am in a position to know. If the minister can show me any advertisements that were published in newspapers or in the form of posters in that country, I shall gladly withdraw the statement that I made.

I only know that
orders to that effect were given.

There was no quarrel between that gentleman and myself as to who should dictate the patronage. The trouble was that I found something not exactly square, and I did not care whether he was Grit or Tory, his head came off.

I do not question the sincerity of the minister in connection with this matter. So far as I could judge from the correspondence, I should say, that the minister was absolutely correct in the stand that he took. But that does not alter the fact that the whole difficulty was caused by the attitude of a certain gentleman in Regina who said that he had the right to make certain appointments. The minister did not quarrel with this man; he considered it entirely beneath his dignity to do so. I do not say this sarcastically, for I , think the minister acted quite as a minister should. If it had not been for the protest of this gentleman that the Department of Militia had made an appointment over his head, probably the existence of this graft would never have been disclosed. It is quite true that, through the activities of the minister, the stealing of hay and oats in the city of Regina was discovered. It was established before the Davidson Commission that eight carloads of hay had been stolen, and that the way bills of 15 other cars had been forged. I wish to be perfectly fair to the Davidson Commission. I met Sir Charles Davidson on more than one occasion; he is what I would call one of the first gentlemen of the old school in this Dominion of Canada, and I have nothing to say against him. But I do submit that if that investigation in Regina had been pushed a little further, men high up in the Conservative party in that city would have been involved. Moreover, I know that evidence substantiating the charges against these persons was sent to Mr. John Thompson, who acted as counsel on Sir Charles Davidson's Investigation Commission, and that he never made use of the evidence. I may mention also the fact that in Regina

the Government was short-changed to the extent of thousands of bushels of oats. If the investigation had been pushed a little further, it would have been ascertained who was (profiting by the stealing of that oats. The -investigation disclosed the fact that this Government was paying sixty cents a bushel for oats in Regina, while the city of Regina itself was buying oats at the' rate of forty-eight or fifty cents a bushel to feed its own horses. This is one of t'he results of the operation of that honest patronage committee that exists in the city of Regina to-day. If the investigations of the Davidson Commission had been pushed a little further the man Mitchell, who is serving a sentence of three years in jail on a conviction of forgery, would not have been the only goat. There was a young men by the name of D. D. Bennett who got away before Mitchell was tried. For this young man Bennett I am personally sorry. I have known him a great many years; he ought to have known better than to get mixed up with this crowd, and to have committed the acts that he did in connection with hay and oats in Regina. Why was he allowed to get away? Mitchell's evidence and the evidence produced at Mitchell's trial involves him to the hilt; if he came back, conviction would certainly result for an offence against the Criminal Cod^e of Canada. It is rumoured around Regina that he is out of the way for the reason that if he were tried he would not be the only goat. I know that the Minister of Militia has not time to bother about where Bennett is, but I am sure that the officials in his department can easily get the information that is necessary to bring that man back. As a matter of fact, I should be only too glad to furnish the Minister of Militia or any person designated by him with the names. I do not wish to bother the minister himself for he is a very busy man. He has had his hands -full since the war began. I do not wish to flatter him, but I do think we sometimes fail to recognize the weight that has been on his shoulders since the war began. I should not like to have carried that weight myself. The expenditure of such a vast amount of money and the preparation of such a large number of troops for the front is a great responsibility. But there are men in the Government who are paid for seeing that there is honest administration in this country, men whose duty it is to see that those who steal from the Government are brought to justice. I say 
that there is one man who is away from justice at the present time, and I am prepared to furnish the Government with his address, if they want to get this man back to Regina and try him for the offence he has committed.
There are one or two others from Regina that we should like to get.

I am prepared to discuss that with my hon. friend at any time. What has taken place at Regina is not to be compared with what has taken place in Winnipeg, for that is in a class by itself. The hon. member from Selkirk has supported the Manitoba Government ever since he had a vote. As regards the Government of Saskatchewan they are absolutely innocent, as far as I am concerned, until they are proven guilty.
That is a good proviso.

I am sure my hon. friend will be interested to know that before the investigation in Saskatchewan gets through some evidence will develop which will be not far from a man who occupies a prominent place in this Government, the Minister of Public Works. But I am not going into local politics. I rose to protest against the system of party patronage that exists not only in the Militia Department, but in every department of this Government. We had an address from the Minister of Trade and Commerce a few days ago, which I think was the gravest indictment of the party patronage system I have ever heard in this House. It strikes me that the present Government are long on promises and short on fulfilment. How the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce can lecture this House on party patronage, and at the same time refuse to raise a finger to stop the riot of patronage in his own department throughout the length and breadth of this country, I cannot very well make out. To bring my remarks to a close, I hope the minister will take steps to clear up the mess in Regina in connection with war purchases during the last year or two.

My hon. friend has made a remark which has already been made by many hon. members on the other side of the House, to the effect that during the present war there has been more partisanship displayed in the awarding of contracts than ever before in the history of Canada. I do not know what has taken place in other ridings, but I hope the House will permit me to tell what has taken place in my own. Whatever party patron-

age there is in the county, is very largely in the hands of the local member. In my own riding seven contracts have been awarded during the war. The first contract was to William Kennedy & Son. They are one of the largest iron and steel manufacturers in Ontario. The head of the firm is Mr. Matthew Kennedy, a brother of Sir John Kennedy, of Montreal. Matthew Kennedy was the Liberal candidate in North Grey, and was defeated by Mr. T. I. Thompson, who took the place of the late Dr. Horsey. William Kennedy & Son received a contract-and I think I might say I assisted them in getting it- to the value of $150,000.

Is he a brother-in-law
of the hon. member for St. Antoine?

No, an uncle-in-law.
The next contract was given to the Owen Sound Iron Works, the president of which is Mr. C. A. Fleming.
